A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results in this search yet. In generation 0, all 84 trials in all worlds scored 0, including training success, so the agent never learned to build at all. The recipe settings and network families listed above did not help. One likely trap is the reward: a large brick that covers some wrong cells still earns net positive reward, and the +1 exact-build bonus may never be seen. So the agent needs to judge, for each placement, whether every cell lands at the correct layer. This round uses a small factorial design. A gives the starting network a recipe built from settings never tried (lr 2.5e-3, 512 envs, 1 epoch, gae_lambda 0.8). C uses the same recipe with a new network that reads features at a learned landing layer. B uses that new network with a moderate recipe. Comparing A with C tests the network, and B with C tests the recipe.

### Round 2
All 87 trials so far, across both generations, scored 0 on dev and 0 in training. That includes this round's untried big-batch recipe and the landing-layer gather network. Because every score is zero, seed noise is unmeasured and no idea can be ranked against another. A failure this consistent across recipes and network families points to a shared cause that the network type does not change. My best guess is that the agent learns to choose DONE too early. Early random placements earn negative reward, so DONE (reward 0) has positive advantage and quickly wins, and the agent never reaches the exact-build bonus. Gen 0's fixed -2 DONE bias did not stop this, because the DONE head can still learn at full speed. Test: scale the DONE logit by 0.1, which makes it learn about 10 times slower under Adam. It then acts as a near-constant threshold that placement logits rise above or fall below. I test this on the starting network, on a version with layout-free dense paths added, and on the gather network.

### Round 3
Five trials and 84 trials from generation 0 all scored about 0. The one nonzero result is r2c2 at 0.002 on one seed, which is a single dev design and very likely noise. Training success is still 0, so the agent is not learning to build at all. Generation 0 already covered most of the recipe space and most network families, and the slow DONE threshold did not help on its own (r2c1, r2c3). The landing-layer gather prior also failed and is 4 to 5 times slower. r2c2 is the only weak lead, and what sets it apart is its layout-free paths (a dense path and per-action biases), gamma 0.99 and higher entropy. With 6 trials left, I will refine r2c2 on axes that are still untried: a learning rate above 2e-3, more fresh samples with more gradient steps, and an anchor-agnostic 5x5 head. Any score above 0.001 becomes the new best.

### Round 4
Only r3c3 scored above zero. It added a zero-initialised 5x5 conv per brick type to the placement logits and reached 0.090 dev success (seeds 0.035 and 0.145), with 0.029 training success. Every earlier trial, including recipe changes and the landing-layer gather prior, scored about 0. The likely cause is that this world's action-to-cell mapping (anchor offset, swapped axes or footprint order) differs from the description, and a local window that ignores the anchor can learn the true offset. The two seeds differ by 0.11, so the noise is large. This is the last round, so the aim is the highest 2-seed mean. I propose: (1) make the anchor-free path nonlinear; (2) raise lr to 2e-3, because learning has only just started and the budget gives about 50 updates; (3) a clean net whose main head ignores the anchor, dropping the misaligned pool head and the slow dense path.

## Trial it ended with
name: Anchor-free primary head net
hypothesis: New idea: if the described anchor is wrong, the fixed-footprint pool head gives misplaced features and noise. Its slow dense path wastes parameters. This net drops both. A wider residual trunk (48 channels) feeds a per-type nonlinear head (1x1 to 24 hidden channels, then a grouped 5x5) as the only placement path, with small output init. Slow DONE, the per-action bias and r3c3's recipe are kept. Refuted if it scores at or below 0.090.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: In Round 4 the text suspects a spatial offset: "this world's action-to-cell mapping (anchor offset, swapped axes or footprint order) differs from the description, and a local window that ignores the anchor can learn the true offset." That is the right kind of change, a misalignment between what the agent sees and where bricks land. But it blames the action mapping, not the observed target channels. It never says the shift is 4 rows toward higher y with wrap-around.
